---
title: "API"
description: "Call GX Cloud APIs with a GitHub token or CLI session token."
---

GX Cloud APIs use bearer-token authentication.

For most user-facing integrations, use a GitHub token:

```bash
gh auth status || gh auth login
export GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)"
export GX_API_URL="https://api.gx.run"
```

The `gh auth token` command returns the token from your local GitHub CLI login. If you need to refresh scopes for private repositories, run:

```bash
gh auth refresh -s read:user -s repo
export GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)"
```

Attach the token to requests:

```bash
-H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

GX validates GitHub tokens against the GitHub user API and maps the caller to `github:<id>`. You can optionally add `X-Org-Id: $GX_ORG_ID`; otherwise GX resolves a default org.

## GET /health

Check that the API and database are reachable.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/health"
```

## GET /v1/auth/me

Inspect the authenticated user, org, token label, CLI session, and machine when available.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/auth/me" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

With an explicit org:

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/auth/me" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "X-Org-Id: $GX_ORG_ID"
```

## POST /v1/publish

Publish a GX review bundle. This is what `gx push` sends after it has produced Git branches, commits, sessions, and review metadata.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/publish" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "event": "gx.pr",
    "created_at": 1760000000000,
    "gx_version": "0.0.0",
    "repo": {
      "root_path": "/repo",
      "backend": "jj",
      "remote_url": "https://github.com/org/repo.git"
    },
    "push": {
      "branch_name": "feature/example",
      "head_commit_id": "abc123",
      "github_pull_request_url": "https://github.com/org/repo/pull/123"
    },
    "stack": [],
    "sessions": []
  }'
```

The server stores the publish event, upserts a bookmark, indexes artifacts when configured, and returns review/bookmark metadata.

## GET /bookmarks

List bookmark metadata for sync and review surfaces.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/bookmarks?merge_status=open" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

Filter to one repository:

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/bookmarks?repo_full_name=org/repo&merge_status=open" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

## GET /v1/review/context

Fetch review context for a repo/ref range. The response can include rules, collision hints, hunk links, and indexed snippets.

```bash
curl --get "$GX_API_URL/v1/review/context" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "repoRoot=/repo" \
  --data-urlencode "base=main" \
  --data-urlencode "head=HEAD"
```

## POST /v1/summaries/generate

Generate a PR Summary for a bookmark or event.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/summaries/generate" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bookmarkId":"..."}'
```

Or generate from an event:

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/summaries/generate" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"eventId":"..."}'
```

PR Summary and GitHub PR chat features are paid GX Cloud features.

## POST /v1/extracts

Ingest hunk links and push metadata.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/extracts" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repoRoot": "/repo",
    "refRange": "main..HEAD",
    "headCommit": "abc123",
    "gxVersion": "0.0.0",
    "hunkLinks": [
      {
        "hunkID": "src/app.ts:10-20",
        "file": "src/app.ts",
        "lineStart": 10,
        "lineEnd": 20,
        "tier": 1,
        "confidence": 0.91,
        "authorship": "agent",
        "tool": "codex",
        "model": "gpt-5"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

## POST /v1/sessions

Ingest raw captured session content.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/sessions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "session-123",
    "tool": "codex",
    "model": "gpt-5",
    "content": "redacted transcript text",
    "capturedAtMs": 1760000000000
  }'
```

## GET /v1/activity

Read recent summaries, sessions, and learned rules.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/activity?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

With pagination:

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/activity?limit=20&cursor=$CURSOR" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN"
```

## POST /v1/code-review-history/record

Record review findings so future reviews can retrieve previous decisions and patterns.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/code-review-history/record" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repoFullName": "org/repo",
    "repoRootPath": "/repo",
    "branchName": "feature/example",
    "headCommitId": "abc123",
    "sourceKind": "manual",
    "prompt": "review auth changes",
    "summaryText": "Auth review completed",
    "findings": [
      {
        "title": "Missing validation",
        "summary": "The handler accepts an unchecked token.",
        "filePath": "src/auth.ts",
        "lineStart": 42,
        "severity": "medium",
        "confidence": 0.8
      }
    ]
  }'
```

## POST /v1/code-review-history/search

Search prior review findings for a repo.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/code-review-history/search" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repoFullName": "org/repo",
    "query": "auth validation",
    "filePaths": ["src/auth.ts"],
    "limit": 5
  }'
```

## POST /v1/reported-logs

Upload reported CLI logs for support.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/v1/reported-logs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "gx_version": "0.0.0",
    "os": "darwin",
    "arch": "arm64",
    "repo_root": "/repo",
    "repo_full_name": "org/repo",
    "error": "publish failed",
    "logs": [
      {
        "path": "publish.log",
        "content": "redacted log content"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

## POST /gx/openai/responses

Proxy a valid OpenAI Responses API request through GX Cloud.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/gx/openai/responses" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-5",
    "instructions": "Be concise.",
    "input": "Summarize this change."
  }'
```

## POST /gx/openai/chat-completions

Proxy a valid OpenAI Chat Completions request through GX Cloud.

```bash
curl "$GX_API_URL/gx/openai/chat-completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "messages": [
      { "role": "user", "content": "Summarize this change." }
    ]
  }'
```

===== FILE: get-started/overview.mdx =====
---
title: "Get started"
description: "Install GX and push your first code change"
---

Start with GX when you want coding agents to produce reviewable work instead of one large undifferentiated diff.

The usual path is:

1. Install GX.
2. Sign in with GitHub.
3. Initialize GX in a repository.
4. Generate, inspect, and push a stack.

## Install

> Windows is not supported yet.

### macOS

Install the [Mac app](/download) if you want the menu-bar app to manage local setup for you. The app installs or updates the CLI, installs the `gxg`, `gxs`, and `gxr` shortcuts, and shows local setup status.

### Linux

Install the CLI directly:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://download.gx.run/install.sh | sh
```

After installation, verify that `gx` is on your path:

```bash
gx version
```

The CLI installer places `gx`, `gxg`, `gxs`, and `gxr` in `~/.local/bin`.

## Sign in

GX uses GitHub for identity.

```bash
gx auth login
gx auth status
```

The web app sign-in and CLI sign-in are linked through your GitHub account. After signing in from the CLI, you can see signed-in CLI devices in the web app, including machine name, GX version, last-used time, and session expiry.

## Initialize a repo

Run `gx init` from the repository you want GX to manage.

```bash
gx init
```

Initialization prepares GX in the repo, configures local identity, and sets up capture support for coding-session provenance.

## Set API Keys

The open-source CLI can use model credentials to infer stacks and revisions:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."
```

Set one or both keys before running `gxg` or `gx generate` if you want local stack and revision inference. This path is for the CLI and MCP workflow. Paid pull request features use GX Cloud.

## First stack

After making changes:

```bash
gx generate # gxg
gx status   # gxs
gx push
```

`gxg` looks at the current repo state and the captured coding-session context. It groups the work into reviewable revisions, orders those revisions into one or more stacks, and writes that structure locally.

`gxs` shows what GX found: unstaged files, local stacks, revisions, base branches, and remote state. Use this before pushing so you can catch the wrong split, an unexpected file, or remote divergence early.

`gx push` exports the stack back into Git and GX Cloud. The Git output is normal branches and commits, so GitHub can open pull requests. The GX metadata adds the richer context: revision order, session provenance, summaries, and the review bundle that powers PR features.

## Agent workflow

For simplicity, use the MCP tools and avoid asking agents to run the CLI directly. The MCP is built to support this flow:

```bash
gx sync     # Pulls changes from remote
gx generate # Uses AI to generate organized and semantic commits and branches
gx status   # Checks the status of gx generate and shows any unstaged files
gx push     # Pushes all new stacks to remote and repairs incomplete previous pushes
```

The MCP server runs through the local CLI, so agents use the same GX workflow a human would use from the terminal.

===== FILE: github/overview.mdx =====
---
title: "Interact with GX in Github PRs"
description: "Use paid GX Cloud features to generate PR Summaries and chat with @gx inside GitHub pull requests."
---

GX adds paid review features inside GitHub pull requests.

The CLI can generate and publish stacks locally. GitHub PR Summaries and `@gx` chat run through GX Cloud and require the paid PR feature set.

## PR Summaries

GX can post a PR Summary comment on a GitHub pull request after a stack is published.

The summary is intentionally short. It should tell reviewers:

- what changed
- why it changed
- which files deserve attention first
- which files are mechanical or safe to skim
- what session or agent context is relevant

The goal is to point reviewers to the important parts of the change instead of forcing them to read every line with no context.

## Chat with `@gx`

Mention `@gx` in a PR comment to ask questions about the pull request.

Ask for orientation:

```text
@gx summarize this PR for someone reviewing it cold
@gx which files should I review first?
@gx what is safe to skim?
```

Ask about a specific part of the diff:

```text
@gx explain the auth callback changes
@gx why did the migration file change?
@gx what does this new background job do?
```

Ask for risk or follow-up review:

```text
@gx what is the highest-risk change in this PR?
@gx are there missing tests?
@gx is this related to the previous retry bug?
```

GX answers from available review sources and cites the sources it used.

You can also use `@gx` to override learned rules:

```text
@gx skip rule never use var
@gx do not enforce this migration naming rule
```

When a matching active rule exists, GX retires it and records the override.

## Data sources

GX answers from the current PR first: the published GX revision diffs, changed hunks, file paths, PR comments, and the latest PR Summary.

When available, GX can also use captured coding-session context, indexed codebase context, previous findings, learned rules, and git blame history. Current PR changes remain the source of truth for what changed.

## GitHub App

To post summaries and replies, GX needs GitHub access for the repository. The GitHub App provides installation-scoped access for posting comments and reading PR context.

The local CLI can still generate and push branches without the paid PR feature set. The paid features are the GitHub-hosted review layer: PR Summaries, `@gx` chat, and cloud-backed review context.

===== FILE: gx-sync-contract.md =====
# GX sync contract

Metadata-first sync between GX Cloud (Postgres) and the local gx CLI + jj workspace. Full push payloads are not replayed on every sync.

## What `gx sync` pulls from Postgres

| Field | Source | Purpose |
| ----- | ------ | ------- |
| Bookmark list | `gx_bookmarks` | One row per `(user_id, repo_full_name, branch_name)` |
| `revision` | `gx_bookmarks.revision` | Monotonic counter; local client skips work when already at revision |
| `head_commit_id` | `gx_bookmarks.head_commit_id` | Latest published jj commit for the bookmark |
| `remote_head_sha` | `gx_bookmarks.remote_head_sha` | Last known GitHub branch tip after server push |
| `merge_status` | `gx_bookmarks.merge_status` | `open` \| `merged` \| `closed` — drives home filters |
| `title` | `gx_bookmarks.title` | Display title (user-editable via Console) |
| Session associations | `gx_pr_events.payload.sessions` (latest event) | Immutable session content; links may move between bookmarks |
| New console sessions | Future ingest API | Append-only; same `PushBundle.sessions` shape |

Convex is **not** part of the sync path. The CLI talks to gx-cloud API (Postgres) directly.

## Revision semantics

1. Every successful publish or server-side mutation bumps `gx_bookmarks.revision`.
2. `gx sync` stores the last seen revision per bookmark locally (gx.db).
3. When `remote_revision > local_revision`, the client fetches bookmark metadata and applies catch-up steps below.
4. Full event payloads are fetched on demand (`GET /v1/bookmarks/:id?include_payload=1`), not on every sync poll.

## Local jj catch-up

When `remote_head_sha` differs from the local bookmark tip:

```bash
jj git fetch
# reconcile local bookmark to remote tip before applying new ops
```

If GX Cloud applies server-side jj ops, the client pulls the new tip via fetch rather than replaying ops locally.

## Publish path (today)

Until server jj is production-ready:

- **Publish:** `gx pr` → `POST /v1/publish` → append event + upsert bookmark
- **Sync:** metadata only; no automatic full payload download unless revision changed

Console remains read-only for stack edits until server-side jj operations are reintroduced.

Implemented path (dev):

- `POST /v1/bookmarks/:id/apply` on gx-cloud API (authenticated)
- Server-side jj apply is currently removed.

## Conflict policy

Conflict resolution (divergent local jj vs server revision, concurrent edits) is **out of scope** for this document. See the separate conflict design doc when published. Phases 1–3 do not block on it.

## Bookmark lifecycle (`merge_status`)

| Status | Set by | Console default | `gx sync` catch-up |
| ------ | ------ | --------------- | ------------------ |
| `open` | default on publish | shown | yes, when revision advances |
| `merged` | Console merge bar / GitHub merge detection | hidden (toggle **Merged**) | skipped |
| `closed` | Console **Archive** or `POST /v1/bookmarks/:id/close` | hidden (toggle **Merged**) | skipped |

Rules:

- Publish (`gx pr`) preserves `merged` status. A new publish on a `closed` bookmark reopens it (`open`).
- Merge and archive bump `gx_bookmarks.revision` so clients can detect metadata changes without replaying payloads.
- `gx sync` still lists merged/closed bookmarks to refresh local `merge_status`, but does not run jj catch-up for them.

## Exit criteria (Phase 4)

- One server-side jj operation (e.g. restack) applied in dev
- GitHub branch matches updated bookmark `remote_head_sha`
- `gx sync` receives new revision without full payload replay

===== FILE: gx/mcp.mdx =====
---
title: "MCP Setup"
description: "Configure the GX MCP server so coding agents can generate, inspect, review, sync, and push stacks through the local CLI."
---

The GX MCP server is installed with the CLI. It shells out to your local `gx` binary, so repo state stays on your machine.

## Install GX first

```bash
curl -fsSL https://download.gx.run/install.sh | sh
gx auth login
```

The installer places `gx-mcp` next to `gx` in `~/.local/bin`.

## Register the MCP server

The released CLI installs a stdio MCP server at `~/.local/bin/gx-mcp`. Register that binary with each agent you use.

### Cursor

```bash
cursor mcp add gx -- env GX_BINARY=$HOME/.local/bin/gx $HOME/.local/bin/gx-mcp
```

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add gx -- env GX_BINARY=$HOME/.local/bin/gx $HOME/.local/bin/gx-mcp
```

### Codex CLI and Codex app

For Codex CLI:

```bash
codex mcp add gx --env GX_BINARY=$HOME/.local/bin/gx -- $HOME/.local/bin/gx-mcp
```

Codex CLI and the Codex app both read MCP servers from `~/.codex/config.toml`. You can also add the server manually with absolute paths:

```toml
[mcp_servers.gx]
command = "/Users/YOU/.local/bin/gx-mcp"

[mcp_servers.gx.env]
GX_BINARY = "/Users/YOU/.local/bin/gx"
```

On Linux, use `/home/YOU/.local/bin/gx-mcp` and `/home/YOU/.local/bin/gx`.

### Other MCP clients

Other clients use the same stdio command shape:

```bash
env GX_BINARY=$HOME/.local/bin/gx $HOME/.local/bin/gx-mcp
```

## Agent workflow

Agents should use GX tools instead of hand-writing Git commands.

| Tool | CLI command | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gx_sync` | `gx sync` | Reflect remote GitHub and GX state locally |
| `gx_generate` | `gx generate --json` | Generate revisions from a session-isolated workspace |
| `gx_status` | `gx status --json` | Inspect unstaged work, stacks, revisions, and remote state |
| `gx_push` | `gx push [stack]` | Push generated branches, commits, sessions, and metadata |
| `gx_review` | `gx review [prompt]` | Review changes using local and cloud context |

The normal flow is `gx_generate`, then `gx_status`, then `gx_push`. Use `gx_sync` first when the agent needs fresh remote state or when a push reports remote divergence.

===== FILE: gx/overview.mdx =====
---
title: "CLI"
description: "Use the open-source gx CLI to generate stacks and revisions, inspect status, review changes, and publish normal Git output."
---

`gx` is the local CLI. It is open source and runs on your machine. It adds a quality and workflow layer around your existing repo instead of replacing GitHub.

GX still produces ordinary Git branches and commits as output. The difference is that GX models the work first as reviewable revisions inside ordered stacks, with captured session context attached.

## gx init

```bash
gx init
```

Prepares the current repository for GX. It configures local identity, initializes GX workflow state, and sets up capture support for coding-session provenance.

Run it once per repository:

```bash
gx init
```

## gx generate

```bash
gx generate
```

Turns current working-copy changes into reviewable stacks and revisions. This is the main command agents should use after making code changes.

`gx generate` is built for messy work: it inspects changed hunks, structural signals, dependencies, and session context, then saves the work in an order that is easier to review.

You can also generate only part of the current diff:

```bash
gx generate src/auth.ts --exclude "**/*.test.ts"
```

## gx status

```bash
gx status
```

Shows the current GX state: unstaged changes, local stacks, revisions, and remote sync status.

Use this after `gx generate` to inspect what GX created before pushing.

Machine-readable output:

```bash
gx status --json
```

## gx push

```bash
gx push
```

Publishes generated stacks. GX pushes normal Git branches and commits, uploads linked sessions and review metadata, and prints GitHub/Review URLs when available.

Run this when the generated revisions look ready to share.

## gx sync

```bash
gx sync
```

Fetches remote Git and GX state before generating or pushing. Use it when GitHub moved, a branch was merged, or `gx push` reports remote divergence.

Recommended agent flow starts with sync:

```bash
gx sync
gx generate
gx status
gx push
```

## gx review

```bash
gx review
```

Reviews local changes using codebase context, captured sessions, review resources, and optional prompt guidance.

You can ask for a focused review:

```bash
gx review "check auth rollback risks"
```

## gx add

```bash
gx add -m "describe this revision"
```

Records the current work as a specific revision with the message you provide. Use this when you already know the exact revision boundary.

For most agent workflows, prefer `gx generate`; it can infer stacks and revision boundaries for messy changes.

## gx edit

```bash
gx edit <revision>
```

Re-enters an existing revision so you can continue working on it. With no revision argument, GX can show a picker of recent mutable changes.

Use this for targeted repair after a generated revision needs follow-up.

## gx doctor

```bash
gx doctor
```

Checks local GX setup and workflow state. Use it when capture, auth, or repository setup looks wrong.

Some safe repairs can be run with:

```bash
gx doctor --fix
```

## gx auth

```bash
gx auth login
gx auth status
```

Signs the CLI into GX through GitHub and shows the current auth state. Web app sign-in and CLI sign-in are linked by your GitHub account.

## gx version

```bash
gx version
```

Prints the installed GX version.

Machine-readable output:

```bash
gx version --json
```

## Shortcuts

The CLI installer also installs three shortcuts:

```bash
gxg # gx generate
gxs # gx status
gxr # gx review
```

They are symlinks to the same `gx` binary. When the binary starts as `gxg`, `gxs`, or `gxr`, it dispatches to the matching command.

## Advanced commands

GX also includes advanced commands for diagnostics, capture, and support.

Use these when needed:

```bash
gx report
gx capture sync
gx ops
```

- `gx report` sends logs to support.
- `gx capture sync` uploads pending captured session data.
- `gx ops` groups advanced capture, diagnostics, and ingest commands.

## Model credentials

The open-source CLI can use provider credentials for local stack and revision inference:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."
```

Use these when you want local CLI/MCP inference to use your own OpenAI or Anthropic credentials. Paid pull request features run through GX Cloud.

---
title: "How it works"
description: "Understand why using gx can improve your workflow"
---

Many changes that happen during a coding session are otherwise lost. Those
details can help teammates and other agents understand the intent and decisions
behind the work. Alongside Git history and other resources, GX gives your team a
stronger review system for moving faster while maintaining high-quality
software.

## The problem

Git was not built for LLMs. Git works great for humans, where you can attach a
message to code changes to review later, but with AI we now have additional
artifacts, like session context, that can save work in an organized way and
supplement your pull requests.

Many changes that happen during a coding session are otherwise lost. Those
details can help teammates and other agents understand the intent and decisions
behind the work.

The second problem is that code review is beoming more of a bottleneck. The cost
to generate code is quickly dropping to zero, while teams still require developers
to review code changes manually, reading line by line.

## The Benefits of GX

Alongside Git history and other resources, GX gives your team a
stronger review system for moving faster while maintaining high-quality software.
GX records your session context (alongside other context resources) to supplement
both your git record and context for pull requests.

In any coding session, you might request changes to multiple areas of code, and it can be hard
to unravel that work into reasonable commits. Many will yolo commits using their codegen, and
while this does save your work, we can leverage VCS systems to help create a database to better
understand changes for our codebase indefinitely.

In short, GX saves your coding session and organizes your work by creating [hunks](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Interactive-Staging)
(Think of a hunk like several lines of code vs. storing an entire file in a commit). This context is
stored in metadata and is saved using GX.

Because work is saved in hunks with clear descriptions alongside the coding session, we can extract
the most important parts of the code changes to review, shortening review time. This removes
the bottleneck of code review while providing a reiable system of record.


## What are stacks and revisions?

You are likely used to git mental model, of branches and commits. These work great, but become
unwieldy if you need to edit a commit, rebase, or do more involved work.

Think of a revision as anologous to a commit. The main difference is that a revision can easily be edited and updated.
A collection of revisions are collected in a stack. Think of a stack as analogous to a branch, but with metadata.

Stacks allow to easily stack PRs and organize our code changes in a way that we can improve review.

While GX maintains these artifacts, when you use `gx push` to push your changes to remote, GX pushes branches and commits,
so your git log stays up to date, and we can easily interface with Github.

## Replace your git workflow

Instead of manually creating a branch and commit:

```bash
git checkout -b feature/my-change
git add .
git commit -m "update stuff"
git push
```

Start with:

```bash
gx generate # alias `gxg`
gx status # alias `gxs`
gx push
```

`gx generate`, or `gxg` generates stacks and revisions. When this command is completed, you will have branches and commits generated for your work.
`gx status`, or `gxs` shows the current status. This shows the output stacks from gxg alonside stacks that have been pushed to remote. This also shows any unstaged files.
`gx push` publishes code changes, alongside session data & metadata, to both gx and Github.

The recommended way to use GX with through the MCP instead of through the CLI. This allows you to generate and save your work through your codegen tool and not touch the terminal.

GX helps teams understand and review AI-written code without treating every pull request as an isolated diff.

The open-source `gx` CLI captures coding sessions, turns messy working-copy changes into ordered revisions and stacks, and publishes those stacks as normal Git branches and commits. The paid GitHub features add PR summaries and `@gx` chat inside GitHub pull requests.

## Start here

- [Get started](/get-started/overview): install GX, sign in, and publish your first stack.
- [How it works](/how-it-works/overview): why GX stores more context than Git and why GX says stacks and revisions.
- [gx](/gx/overview): CLI commands, shortcuts, and the MCP Setup path.
- [Pull Requests](/github/overview): PR Summaries, `@gx` chat, and paid GitHub review features.

## Core workflow

Most users and agents should start with:

```bash
gx generate
gx status
gx push
```

The shortcuts are:

```bash
gxg # gx generate
gxs # gx status
gxr # gx review
```

## Product model

GX uses a few terms consistently:

- **Session**: captured coding context from an agent, editor, or shell.
- **Revision**: one reviewable logical change, including the code diff and the context that explains how it was produced.
- **Stack**: an ordered line of revisions that should be reviewed together.
- **Review bundle**: the published payload that joins code changes, sessions, metadata, and review evidence.

GX still outputs normal Git branches, commits, and pull requests. The GX terms describe the product model before it is exported to Git.

A Git commit is a durable snapshot plus a short message. That is still useful, but it is often too thin for AI-generated work: the commit does not know which agent session produced it, which prompt or shell commands mattered, whether the change was split out of a larger messy workspace, or how it relates to nearby generated work.

A GX revision is the review unit. It can become a Git commit, but it carries richer review context around that commit: session provenance, generated summary, file-level intent, and its position in the stack. Calling it a revision keeps the focus on reviewable evolution of the work, not only on the final Git object.

A Git branch is a pointer in a repository. A GX stack is the product shape of the work: ordered revisions, their dependencies, and the context needed to understand them. GX exports stacks to branches because GitHub and Git still expect branches, but agents and reviewers work better with stacks because they can see the sequence of intent instead of only the final branch state.
